entry: Phylum of simple aquatic [[Invertebrate|invertebrates]], nearly all living in sedentary colonies and also called moss animals. Each individual, or zooid, is typically about 0.5 millimeters (1⁄64 in) long and feeds with a lophophore, a "crown" of tentacles used for filter feeding. Colonies take forms including fans, bushes and sheets. Most marine species live in tropical waters, though some occur in [[Oceanic trench|oceanic trenches]] and polar waters, and a few prefer [[Brackish water|brackish water]]. Freshwater species produce statoblasts that lie dormant until conditions improve. Predators include [[Starfish|starfish]] and sea urchins. The earliest mineralized skeletons date from the early [[Cambrian]]. Larvae undergo a radical [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]] after settling. The invasive species *Membranipora membranacea* has reduced [[Kelp|kelp]] forests off the coasts of the U.S.

Form of plague caused by the bacterium *Yersinia pestis* and usually spread by infected [[Flea|fleas]]. Symptoms appear one to seven days after exposure and include fever, headache, vomiting and swollen, painful lymph nodes called buboes. Without treatment, plague kills 30% to 90% of those infected, typically within 10 days. [[Antibiotic|Antibiotics]] such as streptomycin, gentamicin or [[Doxycycline]] reduce the risk of death to around 10%. Plague is considered the likely cause of the [[Black Death]], which swept through Asia, Europe and Africa in the 14th century and killed an estimated 50 million people.

Capital and largest city of [[Romania]], on the River Dâmbovița in the southeast. Its population is officially estimated at 1.71 million, within a metropolitan area of 2.33 million that makes it the fifteenth-largest city in Europe. The city covers 239 sq km (92 sq mi) and is an enclave surrounded by Ilfov County. First mentioned in 1459, it became a center of [[Wallachia|Wallachian]] commerce and governance in the 16th and 17th centuries, and the capital of the Romanian United Principalities in 1862. Known for its cosmopolitanism and eclectic architecture, it was nicknamed "Paris of the East" before severe damage in World War II. Under socialist rule it grew greatly, notably through [[Nicolae Ceaușescu]]'s program of systematization. Bucharest is now the richest capital in the region, having surpassed [[Budapest]] since 2017.

Official residence and administrative headquarters of the British monarch in [[London]]. Built as a townhouse for the Duke of Buckingham and Normanby in 1703, it was acquired by [[George III]] in 1761 and became the monarch's London residence on the accession of [[Queen Victoria]] in June 1837. John Nash and Edward Blore enlarged it in the early 19th century. Its East Front contains the balcony from which the royal family traditionally greets crowds. The palace has 775 rooms, and a German bomb destroyed its chapel during World War II.

Ceremonial county of South East England, abbreviated Bucks. It is bordered by [[Greater London]] to the south-east, and its largest settlement is [[Milton Keynes]]. The county covers 1,874 sq km (724 sq mi) and had an estimated population of 884,656 in 2024. The Chiltern Hills, an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, occupy the south and contain its highest point, Haddington Hill, at 267 m (876 ft). In the 19th century, [[Cholera|cholera]] and [[Famine|famine]] drove many rural residents to larger towns. Cheap land then attracted London commuters.

American architect, systems theorist, designer and futurist. He popularized the geodesic dome and coined or popularized terms including Spaceship Earth, Dymaxion, ephemeralization, synergetics and tensegrity, publishing more than 30 books. He was awarded 28 United States patents and many honorary doctorates. He attended [[Harvard University|Harvard]] but was expelled in his first year. Dissatisfied with how [[Geometry|geometry]] was taught in school, he developed the ideas behind his later work on synergetics. He served as the second World President of Mensa International from 1974 to 1983 and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President [[Ronald Reagan]] in 1983. [[Carbon|Carbon]] molecules known as fullerenes were later named for their resemblance to geodesic spheres.

Cage-like allotrope of [[Carbon|carbon]] with the formula C₆₀. Its 60 carbon atoms form a truncated icosahedron of 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons, resembling a football, and each atom bonds to three neighbors. The black solid dissolves in hydrocarbon solvents to form a purple solution. Discovered in 1985, it has been intensively studied, though few real-world applications have been found. Molecules are commonly nicknamed buckyballs. The molecule is named after [[Buckminster Fuller]], whose geodesic domes it resembles. Small quantities occur in [[Soot|soot]], and it has been observed in space.

Annual flowering plant of the knotweed family, cultivated for its grain-like seeds and as a cover crop. Common buckwheat (*Fagopyrum esculentum*) is not closely related to wheat or to grasses; it is related to sorrel, knotweed and rhubarb. Its high [[Starch|starch]] content allows the seeds to be cooked like a [[Cereal|cereal]], making it a pseudocereal. Cultivation began around the 6th millennium BC in what is now [[Yunnan|Yunnan]] Province in southwestern China. It was domesticated in inland Southeast Asia, possibly around 6000 BC, and spread to Central Asia, [[Tibet|Tibet]], the Middle East and Europe, which it reached by the 15th century. Buckwheat grows well in low-fertility or acidic soils, and too much [[Fertilizer|fertilizer]], especially nitrogen, reduces yields. Some people, especially in Japan, have serious allergies to it.

Capital and largest city of [[Hungary]], on both banks of the [[Danube|Danube]] River. It is Hungary's political, economic and cultural center, with 1.7 million inhabitants in the city and about 3.3 million in its metropolitan area. Formed in 1873 by the unification of Buda, Pest and Óbuda, the city became a royal seat in 1361. Its historic center along the Danube is a [[World Heritage Site]], with monuments including the Hungarian Parliament and Buda Castle. Budapest is considered the spa capital of Europe, with more than 100 medicinal geothermal springs. Its more than 30 [[University|universities]] enroll over 150,000 students, and the city opened the first underground transit line in continental Europe in 1896.

Collections of Buddhist sacred scriptures, some called *Tipiṭaka* in [[Pali|Pali]] or *Tripiṭaka* in [[Sanskrit|Sanskrit]], meaning three baskets. In ancient India, several canons were organized into three divisions: *Vinaya* (monastic rules), *Sutra* (teachings of [[The Buddha|the Buddha]]) and *Abhidharma* (systematic scholastic works). Many early Indian schools had canons with four or five divisions instead. The [[Theravada|Theravada]] canon of Southeast Asia is written in Pali. The Chinese Buddhist Canon, known in [[East Asia|East Asian]] Buddhism as the Great Storage of Scriptures, is written in Buddhist Chinese, and the Tibetan Buddhist Canon is written in Classical Tibetan. The Sanskrit canon of [[Nepal]] preserves many Sanskrit manuscripts and has been important for modern scholarship.

Philosophical system developed by Buddhist schools in ancient India and later across Asia. Buddhist philosophers have examined [[Cosmology|cosmology]], [[Ethics|ethics]], [[Epistemology|epistemology]], [[Logic|logic]], [[Metaphysics|metaphysics]], ontology, phenomenology and the philosophy of mind. Early texts describe the [[The Buddha|Buddha]] as declining to answer some metaphysical questions because they were irrelevant to liberation, although doctrines such as dependent arising, [[Karma|karma]] and rebirth carry metaphysical implications. Edward Conze divided Indian Buddhist philosophy into three phases: pre-sectarian doctrines, scholastic Abhidharma texts beginning in the 3rd century BCE, and *Mahāyāna* schools from the late first century CE. A recurrent theme is the search for a Middle Way between extreme views.

American singer, songwriter and guitarist, a pioneer of [[Rock and roll|rock and roll]]. Born Charles Hardin Holley in Lubbock, Texas, he formed the Crickets, a band name chosen to get around the limits of his Decca Records contract. Recorded with producer Norman Petty, the single "That'll Be the Day" topped the U.S. and U.K. singles charts in 1957, followed by "Peggy Sue". Holly is often regarded as the artist who defined the rock-and-roll lineup of two guitars, bass and drums. He was among the first inductees into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1986. His work influenced [[Bob Dylan]], [[The Beatles|the Beatles]], [[Eric Clapton]] and [[Elton John]]. He died in a plane crash that also killed [[Ritchie Valens]] and The Big Bopper.

Small, long-tailed, seed-eating [[Parrot|parrot]] native to Australia (*Melopsittacus undulatus*), also known as the budgie or common parakeet. The wild form is green and yellow with black scalloped markings, while captive birds are bred in blues, whites, yellows and grays, and some have small crests. Budgerigars are nomadic flock birds that breed opportunistically and in pairs. They are found throughout the drier parts of [[Australia|Australia]], where they have survived harsh inland conditions for over five million years. Wild birds average 18 cm (7 in) long and weigh 30–40 g. They are the third most popular pet in the world, after the [[Dog|dog]] and [[Cat|cat]], valued for their small size, low cost and ability to mimic human speech.

Capital and most populous city of [[Argentina]], on the southwestern shore of the [[Río de la Plata]]. The city proper has 3.1 million residents, and its urban area has 16.7 million, making it the 21st most populous metropolitan area in the world. It is classified as an Alpha− [[Global city|global city]] in the 2024 GaWC ranking. The city is an autonomous district, separate from Buenos Aires Province, after its federalization in 1880 following the Argentine Civil War. Since the 19th century it has received millions of immigrants, making it one of the most diverse cities in the Americas. Greater Buenos Aires is the fourth-most populous metropolitan area in the Americas and the second-largest city south of the [[Tropic of Capricorn]].

City in western New York State, on the eastern shore of [[Lake Erie]] (pop., 2020: 278,349), at the head of the Niagara River on the Canada–United States border. Selected as the terminus of the [[Erie Canal]] in 1825, it became the world's largest grain port in that era and later the second-largest railway hub in the U.S., after [[Chicago]]. Steel production dominated its economy until deindustrialization and the opening of the [[St. Lawrence Seaway]] led it to diversify into health care, education and tourism.

American supernatural horror drama television series created by [[Joss Whedon]]. It aired on The WB from March 10, 1997, to May 22, 2001, and then on UPN until May 20, 2003. It follows Buffy Summers, played by [[Sarah Michelle Gellar]], the latest in a line of young women who battle [[Vampire|vampires]] and demons in Sunnydale, a small [[Southern California]] city built on a Hellmouth. The series received critical acclaim, and original airings often reached four to six million viewers. It spawned hundreds of tie-in products, including novels, comics and video games.

Cartoon rabbit created in the late 1930s at Warner Bros. Cartoons and the mascot of [[Warner Bros. Pictures|Warner Bros.]] Voiced originally by [[Mel Blanc]], he starred in more than 160 short films between 1940 and 1964 and became a central figure of the *Looney Tunes* series. Typically an anthropomorphic gray-and-white rabbit with a Brooklyn accent, he outwits foes such as Elmer Fudd and Yosemite Sam. His rivalry with [[Daffy Duck]] is friendly, and his catchphrase is "What's up, doc?" He has a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

American mobster who was a driving force behind the development of the [[Las Vegas Strip]]. A founder and leader of Murder, Inc., he was a bootlegger during Prohibition and later ran illegal gambling. He worked with [[Meyer Lansky]] in the [[Organized crime|organized crime]] syndicate. In [[Las Vegas]] he took over the stalled Flamingo Hotel project, whose casino opened on December 26, 1946. Partners believed about US$1 million of the construction budget had been skimmed, and Siegel was shot by a sniper through a window of his girlfriend's Beverly Hills mansion.

Family of medium-sized [[Passerine|passerine]] [[Songbird|songbirds]], Pycnonotidae, found across most of Africa, the Middle East and tropical Asia. The family includes 161 species in 28 [[Genus|genera]], among them greenbuls, brownbuls, leafloves and bristlebills. African species are predominantly found in [[Rainforest|rainforest]], whereas Asian bulbuls mostly inhabit more open areas. Bulbuls feed predominantly on fruit, and also take insects, nectar and small invertebrates, especially while raising young. Most species build cup-shaped nests in trees or shrubs. The red-vented bulbul (*Pycnonotus cafer*) has been introduced to parts of the Americas, [[Hawaii|Hawaii]] and [[Australia|Australia]], where it can become invasive.

Country in southeastern Europe, on the eastern Balkan Peninsula, west of the [[Black Sea|Black Sea]]. Its capital and largest city is [[Sofia|Sofia]]. Covering 110,994 sq km (42,855 sq mi), it is the tenth-largest country in the [[European Union|European Union]]. The First Bulgarian Empire, recognized by treaty in 681 AD, significantly influenced Slavic cultures, including through the [[Cyrillic script|Cyrillic script]]. The region fell under [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] rule in 1396 for nearly five centuries, and independence was declared in 1908. From 1946 Bulgaria was a socialist state in the [[Eastern Bloc|Eastern Bloc]], until the Communist Party gave up its monopoly on power after the revolutions of 1989. It has been a parliamentary republic since adopting a democratic constitution in 1991, and it is a member of [[NATO|NATO]], the eurozone and the Schengen Area.

[[Eating disorder]] marked by binge eating followed by compensatory behavior, such as self-induced vomiting or fasting, to prevent weight gain. Bulimia is more common among people with a close relative who has the condition, and the percentage risk estimated to be due to genetics is between 30% and 80%. Other risk factors include psychological stress, cultural pressure to attain a certain body type, poor self-esteem and [[Obesity|obesity]]. Complications can include dehydration and abnormal heart rhythms that may lead to [[Cardiac arrest|cardiac arrest]]. Diagnosis is difficult because people are usually secretive, and [[Anorexia|anorexia nervosa]] takes diagnostic precedence.

Breed of dog in the [[Terrier|terrier]] family, originating in [[England]]. Originally bred for vermin control and bloodsports, the modern breed was developed by James Hinks in the mid-19th century. The Bull Terrier has a distinctive egg-shaped head and small, triangular eyes. White bull terriers have a strong tendency toward deafness: it occurs in 20.4% of pure white Bull Terriers and 1.3% of colored ones. Lethal acrodermatitis, a rare inherited disease, is found only in white Bull Terriers and is usually fatal, appearing within the first few weeks of life.

Species of requiem [[Shark|shark]] (*Carcharhinus leucas*) found in warm, shallow coastal waters worldwide and known in Africa as the Zambezi shark. It tolerates both salt and fresh water and travels far up rivers, having been recorded as far as Alton, Illinois, about 1,100 km (700 mi) from the ocean on the [[Mississippi River|Mississippi River]]. Adult females average 2.4 m (8 ft) long and typically weigh 130 kg (290 lb). Its aggressive nature has led to shark culling near beaches, and it is listed as vulnerable by the IUCN.

British breed of stocky, muscular [[Mastiff|mastiff]]-type dog, also called the English Bulldog. [[Selective breeding|Selective breeding]] for its flat face and wrinkled skin has increased susceptibility to brachycephaly, hip dysplasia and heat sensitivity, and the breed is illegal to breed in the Netherlands because of concerns about its quality of life. The modern breed was developed as a companion from the Old English Bulldog, which was used for bull-baiting until the sport was outlawed under the Cruelty to Animals Act of 1835. In 2013 it was the twelfth-most frequently registered breed worldwide.

Body armor that protects the torso from firearm projectiles and explosion fragments. Soft vests, worn by police, security personnel and prison guards, protect against stabbing and light projectiles. Hard vests incorporate metallic or para-aramid components and are typically worn by soldiers against rifle ammunition. Trauma plates protect against blunt force, and ceramic inserts stop high-caliber rounds. Early ballistic protection used [[Cotton|cotton]] and [[Silk|silk]]. In the 1860s [[Joseon|Joseon]] Korea developed a soft vest called *myeonje baegab*, after researchers found that 10 layers of cotton fabric could stop bullets. During the [[English Civil War|English Civil War]], [[Oliver Cromwell|Oliver Cromwell's]] Ironside cavalry wore musket-proof cuirasses of two layers of armor plating. Modern vests use advanced fibers such as [[Kevlar|Kevlar]] and ceramic plates.
